title: Climate rationale and baseline
body_markdown:
## Climate rationale and baseline

### Climate hazards and observed trends

Harbor Point faces extreme heat and stormwater flooding. The city recorded 23 days above 35 °C in 2025, compared with an average of 9 such days per year between 1991 and 2020. Heat-related emergency department visits rose from 140 in 2021 to 310 in 2025.

Street flooding affects 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event. The Canal Street underpass closed 6 times in 2025 because of standing water.

### Exposed people and assets

Harbor Point has 182,400 residents. The proposed plan focuses on Eastside and Millbrook, where tree canopy is 11 percent and 13 percent respectively—the lowest levels in the city. The plan identifies street flooding at 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event and records six 2025 closures of the Canal Street underpass because of standing water.

[Information needed: Provide the number of people in Eastside and Millbrook currently exposed to extreme heat and stormwater flooding.]

### Baseline conditions

The existing drainage network in Eastside was designed for a 5-year storm and is undersized for current rainfall intensities. Without the proposed plan, no source-supported projection of future extreme-heat conditions is available.

title: Project components and activities
body_markdown:
## Project components and activities

The Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan comprises three complementary components to reduce extreme-heat exposure and street flooding in Harbor Point between 2027 and 2032.

### Component 1: Cool corridors

The plan will plant 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors connecting schools, clinics, and transit stops in Eastside and Millbrook. The target is to achieve 25 percent tree canopy in both neighbourhoods by 2032. Cool-corridor planting and three years of establishment watering are estimated to cost USD 9.6 million.

Millbrook Neighbours Alliance will co-design cool-corridor routes with residents.

### Component 2: Green stormwater infrastructure

The plan will build 85 bioretention cells and convert 3.2 hectares of asphalt schoolyards into permeable green play areas. These measures are designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface. Green stormwater infrastructure, including design and construction supervision, is estimated to cost USD 14.2 million.

The Department of Public Works will deliver green stormwater infrastructure, and Harbor Point Unified School District will host schoolyard conversions.

[Information needed: Confirm the locations of the 85 bioretention cells under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

[Information needed: Confirm the schoolyard locations for the 3.2 hectares of permeable green play areas under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Component 3: Community cooling network

The Office of Climate Resilience will designate 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres. The centres will have extended opening hours on days above 32 °C. The community cooling network is budgeted at USD 2.7 million from the city operating budget.

[Information needed: Confirm the locations of the 18 community cooling centres under the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

body_markdown:
## Expected results and indicators

### Expected adaptation results

The Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan is intended to reduce extreme-heat exposure and street flooding between 2027 and 2032. In Eastside and Millbrook, the plan targets 25 percent tree canopy by 2032, compared with current canopy cover of 11 percent and 13 percent respectively.

The plan will plant 4,800 street trees along 12 cool corridors connecting schools, clinics, and transit stops in Eastside and Millbrook. It will build 85 bioretention cells and convert 3.2 hectares of asphalt schoolyards into permeable green play areas; together, these measures are designed to capture the first 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface. The Office of Climate Resilience will designate 18 community cooling centres in libraries and recreation centres, with extended opening hours on days above 32 °C.

[Information needed: Confirm the number of direct beneficiaries of the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.]

### Indicators, baselines, and targets

The Office of Climate Resilience will publish an annual progress report. The plan identifies tree canopy cover, the number of flooded intersections during monitored storms, and heat-related emergency department visits as indicators.

| Indicator | Baseline | Target |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tree canopy cover in Eastside | 11 percent | 25 percent by 2032 |
| Tree canopy cover in Millbrook | 13 percent | 25 percent by 2032 |
| Street trees planted along cool corridors | Not stated | 4,800 trees along 12 corridors |
| Bioretention cells built | Not stated | 85 cells |
| Asphalt schoolyards converted to permeable green play areas | Not stated | 3.2 hectares |
| Rainfall capture design scope | Not stated | First 25 millimetres of rainfall from 41 hectares of impervious surface |
| Community cooling centres designated | Not stated | 18 centres |
| Flooded intersections during monitored storms | 37 intersections during a 10-year rainfall event | [Information needed: Confirm the target number of flooded intersections during monitored storms for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.] |
| Heat-related emergency department visits | 310 visits in 2025 | [Information needed: Confirm the target number of heat-related emergency department visits for the Harbor Point Heat and Stormwater Resilience Plan.] |

### Beneficiary context

Harbor Point has 182,400 residents. The plan focuses on Eastside and Millbrook, where tree canopy is lowest in the city and where the cool-corridor measures will be implemented.
